What Makes Cannabis Flower Premium? A Shopper's Guide to Top-Shelf Bud

A practical checklist for judging cannabis flower yourself, what top-shelf tiers mean, why THC isn't everything and how to enjoy premium bud on a budget.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 20269 min read

09min readNews & Culture
In this article
  1. What top-shelf weed means at a dispensary
  2. Look: trichomes, bud structure, trim and color
  3. Smell and feel: aroma, drying and moisture
  4. Freshness: harvest and test dates
  5. Lab results: why potency isn't the whole story
  6. Premium flower vs. vapes and concentrates from the same plant
  7. Classic strains worth knowing
  8. Pairing strains with music, just for fun
  9. Getting the most from top-shelf flower on a budget
  10. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • Top shelf is a store's own label for its priciest tier, not a grade set by Michigan, so judge the flower itself.
  • Look for frosty, intact trichomes, careful trim and a strong, specific aroma; skip flower that's dusty dry, damp or smells like hay.
  • Michigan labels show the harvest date and the test date, so you can check freshness before you buy.
  • A higher THC number doesn't automatically mean better flower: label values can vary, and aroma and freshness matter too.
  • Strain names aren't standardized, so rely on the label, the bud and your own notes more than the name.

"Top shelf weed" is dispensary shorthand for the most prized flower in the case, and it usually carries the highest price. But top shelf is a store's own label, not a grade set by Michigan law, so it pays to judge flower yourself. This guide covers what to look for, what to smell and what to check on the label, plus a few classic strains worth knowing and ways to enjoy premium flower without overspending.

What top-shelf weed means at a dispensary

Most dispensaries sort flower into tiers, often called top shelf, mid shelf and value. The store or the brand sets those tiers based on genetics, how the plants were grown and handled, bud size, trim, freshness, potency and demand. No state agency grades flower, so one store's top shelf can differ from another's.

TierWhat it usually meansGood for
Top shelfSought-after genetics, careful handling, whole buds, strong aromaSpecial occasions, trying a cultivar at its peak
Mid shelfSolid quality with fewer extrasEveryday sessions
ValueSmaller buds or shake at a lower priceRolling, cooking and budget days

You'll also hear "craft cannabis." It usually means small-batch flower grown and finished with extra hands-on care, often hand-trimmed. Like top shelf, it's a description, not a regulated term.

At High Society, we work with trusted vendors, and the products on our shelves have passed Michigan's testing standards. Selection varies by store and changes often, so check your store's online menu to compare what's in stock today.

Look: trichomes, bud structure, trim and color

Start with trichomes, the tiny resin glands where the plant makes most of its cannabinoids and aroma compounds. On premium flower they look frosty and intact, with heads that appear cloudy or milky up close. Rough handling knocks them off, so a dull, beaten-up look is a warning sign. Our trichomes guide explains what you're seeing.

Next, look at structure. Some cultivars grow dense, tight buds and others grow airier ones, so density alone isn't a verdict. What matters is that the buds look whole and well formed, not crushed, leafy or full of stems.

Trim tells you about care. A careful trim removes most of the leaf while keeping the bud's natural shape. Hand or machine, the best trims are gentle, since every bump can knock trichomes off.

Color varies with genetics and growing conditions. Bright to deep greens, purple hues and orange or rust-colored pistils are all normal. Brown, gray or fuzzy patches are not, and you should never use flower that shows signs of mold. For a refresher on the parts of the bud, see our cannabis flower 101 guide.

Smell and feel: aroma, drying and moisture

Aroma is one of the most useful clues you have. It comes mostly from terpenes, the same family of compounds behind the scents of citrus, pine and pepper. A 2021 study in Nature Plants found that "indica" and "sativa" labels didn't line up with the plants' overall genetics; they tracked a small number of aroma compounds instead. Your nose often tells you more than the label category does.

Quality flower smells strong and specific, whether that's fuel, fruit, pine or spice. A flat, grassy or hay-like smell can point to rushed drying or old product.

That's where post-harvest care comes in. Flower is dried slowly, then aged in controlled conditions so moisture evens out and the aroma settles; growers call this the "cure." Growers say patient drying and aging give a smoother smoke and a fuller scent.

Feel matters too. Well-dried flower is springy: it breaks apart without turning to dust, and small stems snap rather than bend. Crumbly flower is too dry, while spongy flower may be too wet, which raises the risk of mold.

Michigan cannabis is sold sealed, so you may not get to smell a jar before you buy. Ask your budtender how a batch has been described, and read the label closely.

Freshness: harvest and test dates

Michigan requires cannabis labels to show the harvest date, along with the lab that tested the product and the test date. Those dates are your freshness check. If a package also shows a packaging date, the harvest date is still the one to look for.

Fresher flower generally keeps more of its aroma, since terpenes fade over time. Once it's home, store it in an airtight container away from light and heat. Our guide to reading a cannabis label explains every line on a Michigan package.

Lab results: why potency isn't the whole story

THC percentage is the number most people shop by, but it's a rough guide. Michigan labels list THC and CBD content with a note that actual values may vary by 10%.

Lab numbers can miss by more than that. In a 2023 Colorado study, researchers tested 23 flower samples from 10 dispensaries, and about 70% came in more than 15% below the THC potency on their labels. That study wasn't about Michigan, but it's a reminder to read a label number as an estimate.

A bigger THC number doesn't automatically make for a better experience, either. In a University of Colorado study published in JAMA Psychiatry, regular users given 16% or 24% THC flower didn't show clearly different results on the study's intoxication and impairment measures.

Aroma, freshness and your own tolerance shape how flower feels. If you want more than the label shows, ask whether the brand publishes a certificate of analysis, the full lab report. It typically lists cannabinoids and may include terpenes and contaminant screening results.

Premium flower vs. vapes and concentrates from the same plant

One harvest can become flower, pre-rolls, vape oil and concentrates. Brands often save their most attractive buds for jars of flower and turn other plant material into extracts.

Concentrates and many vapes deliver far more THC per hit than flower. In the same University of Colorado study, people who used concentrates had higher blood THC levels than flower users. Products labeled "live" are typically made from plants frozen fresh at harvest to hold on to more aroma.

Flower offers something those formats don't: the full look, smell and ritual of the plant itself. Concentrates suit experienced consumers, so if you're new to them, start with a much smaller amount than you'd expect.

Classic strains worth knowing

Strain names are handy shorthand, but they aren't standardized. A 2022 study of commercial cannabis across six states found that product labels didn't consistently match the plants' chemistry. Growers can also sell different plants under the same name.

Use these classics as conversation starters, not promises. Selection varies by store and changes often, so check your store's menu for what's available today.

StrainWhat it's known forCommonly described aroma
Jack HererNamed for the late cannabis activist and author Jack HererPine, spice and citrus
Sour DieselA long-running favorite with a sharp, loud noseFuel and sour citrus
OG KushA long-standing classic nameEarthy pine and fuel
Blue DreamA widely grown classic, usually described as a Blueberry and Haze crossSweet berry
Northern LightsOne of the older names still in circulationEarthy and sweet, with pine

You'll notice we haven't listed effects. How a strain feels depends on the batch, the dose and you.

Pairing strains with music, just for fun

Aroma and music both set a mood, so pairing them is a playful way to explore. There's no science behind these matches; think of them as playlist prompts:

  • Citrus and spice, like Jack Herer: upbeat funk, soul or summer pop
  • Fuel and earth, like Sour Diesel or OG Kush: classic rock, blues or boom-bap hip-hop
  • Sweet berry, like Blue Dream: lo-fi beats, neo-soul or indie folk
  • Earthy and sweet, like Northern Lights: ambient tracks, jazz ballads or an old vinyl favorite

For the story of cannabis in jazz, reggae and hip-hop, see our guide to cannabis and music. Enjoy your listening session at home with adults 21 and older, and never drive after using cannabis.

Getting the most from top-shelf flower on a budget

Premium flower doesn't have to be an everyday purchase. A few ways to stretch your budget:

  • Buy small first. Try an eighth of a new top-shelf cultivar before you commit to more.
  • Compare price per gram. Bigger packages often cost less per gram, but only if you'll finish the flower while it's fresh.
  • Mix your tiers. Save top shelf for special sessions and keep a value option for everyday use or cooking.
  • Look at smaller buds. Some brands sell smaller buds from premium batches at a lower price.
  • Store it well so nothing goes stale before you get to it.
  • Join The Society. Our loyalty program is free to join, and members earn points on qualifying purchases. Check current deals before you shop.

Adults 21 and older, and registered medical patients 18 and older, can shop at any of our eight Michigan stores with a valid ID. Enjoy cannabis responsibly.

Frequently asked questions

How can you tell if weed is good quality?

Look, smell and check the label. Good flower is frosty with intact trichomes, carefully trimmed and free of brown, gray or fuzzy spots. It smells strong and specific rather than grassy, and it feels springy rather than crumbly or damp. On a Michigan label, check the harvest date to judge freshness.

What does top-shelf weed mean?

It's a store's name for its premium flower tier, usually its priciest. Stores and brands set those tiers based on genetics, growing and handling, appearance, aroma, freshness and potency. No Michigan agency grades flower, so top shelf at one shop can differ from another. Judge the flower itself, not just the tier.

Is higher THC always better?

No. Label numbers are estimates, and one Colorado study found most flower samples tested well below their labels. Another study found no clear difference in intoxication and impairment measures between 16% and 24% THC flower among regular users. Aroma, freshness and your tolerance matter, so start low with any new product.

What is craft cannabis?

It's an informal term for small-batch flower grown and finished with extra hands-on attention, often including hand trimming and slow drying. It isn't a legally defined category in Michigan, so ask what a brand means by it and judge the flower by its look, aroma and harvest date.

Why does premium flower cost more?

Mostly because it costs more to produce. Premium flower often comes from sought-after genetics, smaller batches, careful handling, hand trimming and longer drying and aging. Demand plays a part too. If the price is a stretch, try a smaller amount, look for smaller buds from premium batches or check current deals.

Sources

  1. Watts S. et al., Cannabis labelling is associated with genetic variation in terpene synthase genes, Nature Plants (2021)pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  2. Smith C.J. et al., The phytochemical diversity of commercial Cannabis in the United States, PLOS ONE (2022)pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  3. Schwabe A.L. et al., Uncomfortably high: Testing reveals inflated THC potency on retail Cannabis labels, PLOS ONE (2023)pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  4. Bidwell L.C. et al., Association of naturalistic administration of cannabis flower and concentrates with intoxication and impairment, JAMA Psychiatry (2020)pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  5. Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency: Marihuana Rules, R 420.1 to R 420.1004 (R 420.504 packaging and labeling)michigan.gov
21+

For adults 21 and older. Keep cannabis away from children and pets, and never drive after consuming. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places.
